summary.text: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a pivot so that it can swing freely back and forth.
Gravity pulls a displaced pendulum back toward its resting position, and the time for one full left-and-right swing is its period.
For small swings the period barely depends on how wide the swing is, which made pendulum clocks the world's standard for timekeeping for centuries.

facts.label: Clock inventor
facts.value: Christiaan Huygens built the pendulum clock in 1656

facts.label: Isochronism
facts.value: Small swings of any width take about the same time

facts.label: Early use
facts.value: A 1st-century earthquake sensor built by Zhang Heng

facts.label: Double pendulum
facts.value: A pendulum hung from another one moves chaotically

items.prompt: A child on a playground swing is pulled back and released. What pulls the swing back toward the middle?

options.label: The pivot pushing outward
A restoring force from gravity
The air pushing on the seat
The weight of the chains alone

items.explain: A displaced pendulum feels a restoring force due to gravity that accelerates it back toward equilibrium.

items.prompt: A grandfather clock's pendulum slowly swings a bit narrower as the day goes on, yet the clock stays on time. Why?

options.label: Narrower swings are timed faster by the clock
The weight of the bob corrects the time
Swings of different widths take about the same time
Friction speeds up the pendulum to match

items.explain: For small swings the period is nearly independent of amplitude, a property called isochronism that makes pendulums useful for timekeeping.

items.prompt: A clockmaker wants to change how long one swing of a pendulum takes. Which part should she adjust?

options.label: The length of the pendulum
The person who started the swing
The side it was first pushed toward
The colour of the hanging weight

items.explain: The period depends on the length of the pendulum.

items.prompt: An ideal pendulum model swings at the same width forever. Why does a real clock pendulum die down without pushes?

options.label: Gravity weakens the longer it keeps swinging
Its restoring force reverses direction over time
The cord slowly shrinks as the pendulum swings
Friction and air drag act on a real pendulum

items.explain: An ideal pendulum has no friction and keeps a constant amplitude, but real pendulums feel friction and air drag, so their swings decline.

items.prompt: A pendulum made of one rod swings with another rod hanging from its end. How does its motion differ from a single pendulum's?

options.label: It becomes chaotic and hard to predict
It swings in a perfectly regular pattern
It cannot swing at all
It always keeps time better

items.explain: A double pendulum, with a second pendulum attached to its end, has chaotic motion.

items.prompt: A scientist wants a physical device that reacts when a distant earthquake strikes. Which old idea relied on a swaying weight?

options.label: A pendulum-based seismometer
A spring-powered clock
A quartz oscillator
A Kater gravity scale

items.explain: One of the earliest known uses of a pendulum was Zhang Heng's seismometer, which swayed to activate a lever when disturbed by an earthquake's tremor.
